chapters.title: Chapter 6: Cash Flow Management in Practice

lessons.title: Early Warning Signs of a Cash Crunch

children.text: Cash crises happen slowly and then suddenly. The sudden part is a bounced cheque, a supplier stopping deliveries, or salaries going out three days late. The slow part runs for six to eighteen months before that, in plain sight, in numbers the company already produces every month. This lesson is about reading that slow part, because almost every option available to a business gets cheaper the earlier it is used.

body.text: By the time a business feels a cash crisis, it has usually been visible in the numbers for a year. The skill is not predicting trouble, it is noticing what is already there.

children.text: Six Quarters of a Company Sliding
Vidarbha Engineering is a fictional component manufacturer. Here is what its board saw every quarter, and what it should have been reading.

body.caption: Vidarbha Engineering: the numbers nobody acted on (days)

body.text: Look carefully at the payables column, because it is the one most often misread. Days payable rose from 45 to 92, and in a board pack that can be presented as successful negotiation with suppliers. It was not. The company was paying late because it could not pay on time, and the stretch was almost exactly keeping pace with its own customers paying late. Rising payables alongside rising receivables is a distress signal, not a treasury achievement.

body.title: Profit rising while operating cash collapses (₹ crore)

stats.label: Profit over six quarters
stats.context: Every quarter better than the last

stats.label: Operating cash over the same period

children.text: Every quarterly review at Vidarbha Engineering opened with a profit chart that went up and to the right. The divergence between the two lines is the single most reliable early warning in business, and it was available from Q2.

body.title: Where the cycle ended up
body.prompt: In Q6, Vidarbha Engineering had 96 debtor days, 98 inventory days and 92 days payable. What was its cash conversion cycle, in days?
body.explanation: 96 plus 98 minus 92 is 102 days, up from 83 in Q1. Note how the stretched payables disguise the damage: without that 47-day stretch, the cycle would have been 149 days. The company was funding a far worse position than the headline cycle suggested, using its suppliers to hide it.

children.text: The Four Places Warnings Show Up
Signals arrive in a rough order, and the later the category, the fewer options remain.

body.caption: Warning signs, from earliest to most serious

cells: DSO, inventory days and the cycle lengthening for two or more quarters, drawing power falling
Operating cash flow falling while profit rises, cash conversion below 1 for several periods
Early, and the most reliable single signal
Cash credit permanently at the limit, frequent excess requests, cheques presented and represented, month-end scrambles
Middle. Options narrowing and getting expensive
Paying suppliers by who shouts loudest, routine early payment discounts to pull cash in, salaries delayed, statutory dues delayed
Late. Each of these costs real money and signals distress outward

body.text: Delaying statutory dues is the most serious signal in the entire list, and it is usually the last one to be admitted. A business that has started using TDS, GST or PF money to fund operations has run out of every cheaper option, is accruing interest and penalties it cannot deduct, and is creating a problem that does not go away when trading improves.

columns.label: A healthy cash position
points: The cash credit balance moves up and down through the month
Suppliers are paid on a fixed run, on agreed dates
The forecast trough is known three months ahead
Collections calls happen before due dates
Statutory payments are funded on the 1st

columns.label: A business in trouble
points: The limit sits at the ceiling every day
Payments are released by whoever calls the promoter
Nobody knows next month's low point
Collections calls start when the supplier calls you
The 7th and the 20th are decided in the same week they fall

body.title: The misread signal
body.textWithBlank: Rising days payable is often presented as better supplier terms, but alongside rising debtor days it usually means the business is paying ___.
body.explanation: Genuine term improvements are negotiated, documented and apply to specific suppliers. A general stretch across the payables book, moving in step with deteriorating collections, means the business is funding itself from whoever will wait, which is the most expensive funding available once MSMED interest and lost input credit are counted.

children.text: The sequence is remarkably consistent across industries and company sizes.

events.title: The cycle lengthens quietly
events.description: A few large customers start paying later. Inventory creeps up because a forecast was optimistic. Nobody notices, because profit is fine.

events.title: Cash credit usage rises
events.description: The limit that used to fluctuate now sits above 80% most days. It is explained as growth.

events.title: Payment behaviour changes
events.description: Supplier payments start being prioritised rather than scheduled. Early payment discounts are offered to customers to pull cash forward.

events.title: The limit is exhausted
events.description: Excess requests to the bank become routine. Drawing power falls because receivables have aged past the eligible window, tightening the limit exactly when it is needed most.

events.title: Statutory dues slip
events.description: GST or TDS is paid late for the first time. Salaries go out two days late. Suppliers begin asking for advances.

events.title: The visible crisis
events.description: A cheque is returned, a key supplier stops delivery, or the account is flagged. Every remaining option is expensive, and most require somebody else's agreement.

body.text: Notice where the options are. At month minus 12, the fixes are ordinary management: collect better, hold less stock, negotiate terms. At month zero, the fixes require a bank, an investor or a buyer to say yes. The cost of waiting is not measured in interest, it is measured in who controls the decision.

body.title: Distinguishing a bad quarter from a deteriorating business

children.text: Not every weak cash quarter is a warning. Panicking at the first divergence is its own kind of mismanagement, so apply three tests.
One quarter is noise. Two or three consecutive quarters moving the same way is a trend. Vidarbha Engineering had five.

A genuine one-off has a story and a date: a festive build-up that unwinds in November, a large order shipping in March, an input price spike that has passed. If nobody can name when it reverses, it is not a one-off.
Does it reverse when it should?

Lesson 1.3 showed Asian Paints converting only about 0.32 times its profit into operating cash in the year to March 2022, which looks alarming in isolation. Across the five years to March 2026, cumulative operating cash was about 1.09 times cumulative profit. The test was not the bad year, it was whether the recovery arrived.

Vidarbha Engineering fails all three: the direction is consistent, no reversal date was ever named, and cumulative operating cash of about ₹1 crore against ₹7.35 crore of profit over six quarters shows the gap never closed.

body.title: Which one would worry you most?
body.question: Four things happen in the same month at a profitable company. Which is the most serious warning?
options: The cash conversion cycle lengthens by 6 days
The cash credit account touches its limit twice
GST for the previous month is paid nine days late
A large customer asks to move from 60-day to 90-day terms
body.explanation: Paying statutory dues late means every cheaper source of funds has already been used. The other three are genuine signals worth investigating, but each has ordinary explanations and ordinary responses available. A late GST payment usually means the money collected on behalf of the government was spent on operations, which places the business much further along the timeline than it realises.

body.title: Your first week at Vidarbha Engineering
body.scenario: You join Vidarbha Engineering as finance manager in Q5. Profit is up for the fifth straight quarter, the promoter is proud of improved supplier terms, the cash credit account has been at its limit for four months, and the auditors raised no concerns last year. Your predecessor left suddenly. Nobody has asked you to investigate anything.
body.prompt: What do you look at in your first week, and what do you say to the promoter?
body.modelAnswer:
Gather the evidence before forming a view, in this order.
1. Pull the last eight quarters of debtor days, inventory days, payable days and the cycle. One afternoon of work, and it produces the table in this lesson.
2. Compare profit against cash from operations for the same period. If cumulative operating cash is well below cumulative profit, the profit is sitting in receivables and stock.
3. Get the receivables ageing by customer and find out what share is beyond 90 days, and which customers account for it.
4. Get the payables ageing, separate micro and small suppliers, and check exposure beyond the MSMED limit. That is interest, disallowance and a filing obligation, not just a payment delay.
5. Look at the daily cash credit balance for six months, not the month-end figure. Month-end numbers are often dressed; the daily pattern tells the truth.
6. Check drawing power against the sanctioned limit and find out which receivables the bank has excluded.
7. Check statutory payment dates for the last twelve months for any late payment, however small.
Then have the conversation, carefully.
8. Lead with the evidence, not the diagnosis. Show the two lines, profit and operating cash, on one chart. It is very hard to argue with.
9. Reframe the supplier terms achievement honestly: payables stretched 47 days while debtors stretched 38, so the company is passing its collection problem down the supply chain. Name the cost of that in MSMED interest and lost input credit.
10. Do not present it as blame or as a crisis. Present it as a window: at this stage the fixes are still ordinary management actions, and they stop being ordinary in about two quarters.
11. Ask for three things: a weekly cash forecast, a collections push on the 90-plus bucket, and a decision on the slow-moving stock. Those three are enough to establish whether the trend can be turned.
12. If the promoter refuses to engage, put the analysis in writing anyway, dated. That is professional obligation, not politics.

body.title: A monthly early warning review
steps: Track debtor days, inventory days, payable days and the cycle every month, and look at the direction over the last six months, not the latest figure.
Plot profit against cash from operations on one chart, cumulatively, and watch for the lines separating.
Review the daily cash credit balance pattern, not just the month-end number.
Check drawing power against the sanctioned limit, and which receivables have aged out of eligibility.
Check the share of receivables beyond 90 days, and whether it is growing.
Check payables beyond the MSMED limit, and any statutory payment made late, however small.
Ask one question about every deterioration: what is the explanation, and on what date does it reverse?
Report the answers to the same people every month, so a trend cannot hide behind a good quarter.

cards.definition: Operating cash flow falling while profit rises. The most reliable early warning available.
Payable days rising across the whole supplier base because the business cannot pay, not because terms improved.
A cash credit account permanently drawn, meaning the revolving facility has become a term loan.
Borrowing capacity shrinking as receivables age out of eligibility, exactly when cash is tightest.
Paying TDS, GST or PF late. The signal that every cheaper option is already exhausted.
The date a one-off explanation says the position will correct. If nobody can name it, it is a trend.

points: Cash crises are visible in company data for six to eighteen months before they are felt.
Profit rising while operating cash falls is the single most reliable warning. Vidarbha Engineering showed it from Q2 and acted in none of the five quarters that followed.
Rising payable days alongside rising debtor days is distress, not negotiation. Stripping out the stretch, Vidarbha's real cycle was 149 days, not 102.
Signals arrive in order: working capital metrics, then profit and cash divergence, then bank behaviour, then payment behaviour.
Late statutory payment is the most serious signal, because it means every cheaper source of funding is gone.
Apply three tests before panicking: direction over several quarters, a named reversal date, and whether the reversal actually happens.

body.text: Vidarbha Engineering is fictional and its figures are illustrative. The Asian Paints comparison uses screener.in data cited in Lesson 1.3 and may be restated later. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation on any security.
